title: "master of the day of judgment"
hook: "master of the day of judgment" — why the second verse is about mercy again

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first line of al-Fatiha. In the name of the merciful, two mercy names before anything else. Did the gentle first sentence help? Day seven.
screen: `AL-FATIHA, LINE 1 — IN THE NAME OF THE MERCIFUL.`

segments.voice: A week ago this started with one word. Salaam. Since then: bismillah, alhamdulillah, inshallah, the five pillars, and the first line of a prayer. Here's something you might not have noticed. Two of those words were already waiting inside that prayer. Bismillah is its first line. And alhamdulillah is the very first word of the next one. So today, as the week closes, we keep walking through al-Fatiha, and the week comes back to meet us. Along with a line that sounds, at first, like a warning.
screen: `ONE WEEK, SIX WORDS.` → `THEY WERE INSIDE THE PRAYER.` → `A LINE THAT SOUNDS LIKE A WARNING.`

segments.voice: After the first line, the prayer goes on. In Pickthall's words: “Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds, The Beneficent, the Merciful. Master of the Day of Judgment.” Those are verses two, three and four of the seven. Listen to what just happened. The Beneficent, the Merciful: the same two names from verse one, said again. Mercy, twice, before the word judgment even appears. Scholars have long read an order in that. A well-known hadith, in Bukhari and Muslim, says that when God created the world, He wrote that His mercy outstrips His anger. The prayer is built the same way. Then the line itself: maliki yawmi d-din. Two details for the curious. The Qur'an has more than one accepted way of being recited, and in some that first word is maalik, owner or master, and in others malik, king. Both are accepted. And din, translated judgment, is also the everyday Arabic word for religion, a way of life. It carries the sense of a debt coming due, an account settled. So this isn't a threat dropped into the middle of a mercy prayer. It's the other half of trust: someone keeps the account, and the one keeping it has just been named merciful, twice. One more thing. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ described al-Fatiha as a conversation, in a hadith qudsi, a saying of God reported by the Prophet, recorded by Muslim. At each of these lines, God answers. At the praise: My servant has praised Me. At the mercy: My servant has extolled Me. At the Day: My servant has glorified Me. Four verses down, three to go.
screen: `VERSES TWO, THREE AND FOUR.` · `MERCY AGAIN, BEFORE JUDGMENT.` · `DIN — A DEBT COME DUE, A WAY OF LIFE.` · `EACH LINE GETS AN ANSWER.` · then, large: `MASTER OF THE DAY OF JUDGMENT.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell, one for each verse today. First breath: praise. For anything at all, even the plain fact that you're here. Second breath: mercy. For someone, and include yourself. Third breath: the account. One thing from this week you'd want to settle well. If you want, the Arabic rides out on the last one: maliki yawmi d-din.
Al-Fatiha, line two. Praise, mercy again, and then the Master of the Day of Judgment. Seventh word, and a full week on your strand.
Your line: mercy twice before anything else. Before you judge anything today, a person, a message, yourself, find two kind things to say about it first. A week, done. Day seven.

howItsDone: Muslims recite these verses in Arabic as part of al-Fatiha in every unit of every prayer; many also pause at the end of each verse, following the Prophet's practice of reciting it verse by verse.

a debt come due, an account settled, and a whole way of life.

fork.setup: al-Fatiha has just said: praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds. what comes right before "Master of the Day of Judgment"?
fork.reveal: the Beneficent, the Merciful: the same names as verse one. mercy twice before judgment ever appears.

original.note: Arabic: "master of the day of judgment." some accepted readings say malik, king, instead of maalik, owner.

trapdoor: what you thought: a warning in the middle of a prayer.
what it means: master of the day of judgment — said only after mercy has been named twice.
what a scholar hears: din is judgment and debt come due, and also "religion." and the first word has two accepted readings: maalik (owner) and malik (king).

notes: This day covers verses 2–4 (Kufan numbering) so the index carry 'mercy twice before anything else' and the hook 'why the second verse is about mercy again' both hold. The index's 'line 2' doesn't match verse numbers; see day 6's note about verse 5.

The index hook says 'the second verse is about mercy again'. That holds if the bismillah is not counted as a verse (then 'The Beneficent, the Merciful' is verse 2). In the numbering most copies print, it's verse 3. The script avoids the ordinal.
Hadith qudsi (Muslim 395): the three answers are paraphrased ('praised Me', 'extolled Me', 'glorified Me'); it's not a quotation from any translation. Confirm number and wording.
'His mercy outstrips (prevails over) His anger' cited to Bukhari 3194 / Muslim 2751 from memory; please confirm.
Readings of 1:4: maaliki (Hafs, the most widely printed) and maliki (Warsh and others). Confirm the examples.
The howItsDone line about pausing at the end of each verse refers to a hadith (Abu Dawud/Tirmidhi) about the Prophet reciting verse by verse; confirm or drop.
Tomorrow's index title 'show us the straight path' is not Pickthall's wording (Pickthall 1:6: 'Show us the straight path'). Fine as a title, but day 8's writer should quote Pickthall, not the title.
Week-end look back is in the hook (the six words so far, and that bismillah and alhamdulillah are inside al-Fatiha).
